findings.title: Stale denial cache entries are never revalidated and take precedence over fresh allows
findings.body: In Check, the permDenialCache is consulted before anything else and short-circuits the entire request, returning Allowed=false. Denial entries live for shortCacheTTL (30s) and are never invalidated or cross-checked against fresher data. Two concrete consequences: (1) a user who is granted permission (directly, via a team, or via a folder) within 30s of a denied check keeps being denied until the entry expires — unlike stale allows in permCache, which now trigger a DB requery on miss, a stale denial has no fallback path to correct itself; (2) deny-wins ordering means a stale denial entry overrides a newer allow already sitting in permCache (e.g. denial cached at t=0, grant at t=5, a DB fetch for another resource refreshes permCache with the allow at t=6, a check at t=7 still returns deny because the denial entry is hit first). This partially re-introduces, on the deny side, the exact staleness problem this PR is fixing for newly created resources. Consider checking the denial cache only after the cached-permission allow path, or validating a denial hit against the current cached permission set before returning it.

findings.title: Denial-cache test would pass even if the denial cache were ignored
findings.body: In TestService_CacheCheck/'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry', the comment says 'Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked', but the code seeds the permission cache with map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false} — a false value, which checkPermission treats as not allowed anyway. As a result the assertion resp.Allowed == false would hold even if the permDenialCache lookup were removed entirely, so the test does not actually prove that the denial cache short-circuits the check. The seeded value should be true so the test fails when the denial entry is not honored.

findings.title: permissionCacheUsage metric recorded as a hit when only the denial cache was used
findings.body: When a Check is answered from permDenialCache, the code increments s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage with label "true" (cache hit), even though the permission cache itself was never consulted. This inflates the apparent permission-cache hit rate and makes it impossible to distinguish permission-cache hits from denial-cache hits in monitoring, which matters when tuning the TTLs this PR introduces. A separate label value or metric for denial-cache usage would keep the signal accurate.
